summary: Children learn to name and use the days of the week and months of the year in order, and to grasp their nested, cyclic structure — 7 days in a week, about four weeks plus a few days in a month, and 12 months in a year, all of which repeat. The main risk is rote recitation (the 'days song') without functional understanding: knowing the chant but unable to say what comes after Thursday or to read a calendar. Guidance targets functional use (random access in both directions), the cycle (the week/year comes round again), and the nesting (days inside weeks and inside months, months inside a year; weeks do not fit into months exactly, so a week can run across two months).
misconceptions: Recites the sequence but can't start from the middle ('what's after Wednesday?') without restarting
Cannot work backwards through the days/months
Doesn't grasp nesting — treats week, month, year as unrelated, or a year as vaguely 'a long time'
Treats the cycle as linear — nothing comes after Sunday or December

activities.title: The looping days wheel: jump in anywhere, go both ways
steps: Spin or turn a days-of-the-week wheel and watch it roll past Sunday straight back to Monday, so the week never 'ends' — it comes round again.
Tap or point to any day (e.g. Wednesday) and name 'the day after' without singing from Sunday.
Answer 'what's after / before X' questions starting from a day in the middle, moving both forwards and backwards.
Optional: tapping a day lights up the day after and the day before so the child can check their answer against the wheel.
activities.insight: The days form a repeating cycle you can enter at any point and travel in either direction — not a one-way song that must restart from the beginning.

activities.title: Zoom from a day to the year: nesting made visible
steps: Start from a single day, then pull back to see the week-row it sits in, then the month-grid that contains that day (noticing that some week-rows run into the month before or after), then the whole year-strip of 12 months.
Place a birthday or seasonal event and say which month it is in and whether that is near the start, middle or end of the year.
Order time-units by length and answer 'which is longer, a week or a month?', explaining how you know.
Optional: a nested visual (day inside week-row inside month-grid inside year-strip) the child can move between to see the containment.
activities.insight: Days sit inside weeks and inside months, and months sit inside a year — the units are related, not separate. A month holds about four weeks plus a few extra days (weeks do not fit into months exactly), so a month is longer than a week.

activities.title: Count across the calendar: dates and weekdays together
steps: Using a real January-style month calendar, start from a given date and weekday (e.g. 'your party is on Saturday the 6th').
Count on across the calendar: 'Three days after the party you go swimming — point to that date and tell me the day.'
Use day-of-week clues to find a date (e.g. 'she visits her aunty on the first Tuesday after the party — which date is that?').
Name both the date and the weekday for the day you land on.
activities.insight: A calendar lets you count across dates and link each date to its weekday, which is using the structure rather than reciting it.

activities.title: Daily calendar talk: functional use in conversation
steps: Join a short daily routine: 'Today is…, yesterday was…, tomorrow will be…'.
Answer an in-role question such as 'what day will it be after the weekend?' or 'what month is your birthday in?'.
Reason aloud from a known day to an upcoming one, connecting days and months to real events (the weekend, birthdays, seasons).
Match months to seasons when a season is mentioned, using the seasons where the child lives (the months for each season differ between the Northern and Southern Hemispheres).
activities.insight: Days and months are tools for talking about real time — when things happened and will happen — not just a list to chant.

activities.title: Order and choose: sequencing and comparison questions
steps: Put the days (or the months) in order.
Answer 'what comes after Thursday?' style questions, including ones that start from the middle of the sequence.
Circle or select the time-units shorter than a week from a set such as 1 year, 1 day, 1 hour, 1 minute, 1 month.
Match months to the seasons they fall in where the child lives (the months for each season differ between the Northern and Southern Hemispheres).
activities.insight: Ordering and length-comparison tasks check that the child knows sequence and relative size, not just the chant.

checkQuestion: Use a real calendar and routine talk, listening for functional USE rather than recitation: (1) 'Today is Wednesday — what day will it be tomorrow? What day was it yesterday?' (2) 'What month is your birthday in? Is that near the start or the end of the year?' (3) Using a January calendar: 'Your party is on Saturday the 6th. Three days after the party you go swimming — point to that date and tell me the day.'
checkAnswer: Names the day after and before Wednesday without reciting from Sunday; places a month within the year (start/middle/end); uses the calendar to count on three days and names both the date and the weekday — showing days sit inside weeks inside months inside the year.
